visuals.heading: Python and the ML Toolkit

items.text: Derivatives and gradients explain how a model actually learns through gradient descent.
Treat calculus as a later unlock, not a entry requirement.
The three areas that matter are statistics and probability, linear algebra, and calculus, and none of them require research-level depth to get started.
This is the math you will use most, day to day: understanding distributions, variance, correlation, sampling, and how to read whether a model result is genuinely meaningful or just noise.
Learn it by applying it inside pandas and scikit-learn on a real dataset, not by working through a standalone theory textbook first.

blocks.heading: Matters More Than Most Beginner Roadmaps Admit

items.text: Get comfortable with Python itself, then pandas and NumPy for cleaning and reshaping real datasets.
Learn distributions, variance, correlation, and basic hypothesis testing by running them on a dataset in pandas, not by memorising formulas in isolation.

visuals.heading: Kaggle Vs a Real Portfolio

items.text: Kaggle hands you the data, the problem, and the metric already defined.
Aim for three to five real, end-to-end projects instead of a long list of small notebooks.
Document each project properly on GitHub: the problem you chose, the options you considered, why you picked the approach you did, and what you would measure to know it worked.
Deploy at least one project somewhere real, even a small hosted API or a simple web app.
Get one honest outside review from someone already working in ML before you lean on a portfolio nobody else has stress-tested.
